interviewQuestions.question: Someone claims their application is secure because it runs in a container. What's wrong with that reasoning?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Containerization solves packaging and deployment consistency, and it does provide real isolation through kernel namespaces and cgroups — but that isolation was designed primarily for resource and process separation, not as a hardened security boundary against a determined attacker who already has code execution. Unlike a VM, a container shares the host's kernel directly; there's no hardware-level virtualization boundary underneath it by default.

That gap is exactly why container-breakout vulnerabilities are a real, recurring category, and why the actual security posture depends on a stack of separate decisions layered on top of the container itself: is the image free of known CVEs, does the container run as non-root with a read-only filesystem, does Kubernetes RBAC limit what the pod's ServiceAccount can do to the cluster, do NetworkPolicies restrict what other pods it can reach. "It's containerized" answers none of those questions.

The concrete failure mode I'd point to: mounting the host's Docker socket into a container hands that container direct control over the host's runtime — a well-documented path to full host compromise that has nothing to do with any vulnerability in the container image, just a configuration choice that voluntarily removed the isolation.

**Testing:** whether you understand containers as a real-but-imperfect boundary rather than an unbreakable security sandbox.

interviewQuestions.question: Walk me through what actually happens when you store a secret in a Kubernetes Secret object, and why teams often route real secrets through a separate secrets manager instead.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
By default, a Kubernetes Secret's value is stored base64-encoded, not encrypted. Base64 is a reversible text-safe encoding — anyone who can read the Secret object through the API, or who has access to the underlying etcd datastore where it's persisted, can decode it with zero cryptographic effort, no key required. It looks obscured when you glance at a manifest, which is exactly what makes people assume it's protected.

Kubernetes does support encryption at rest for etcd, but it's a separate, explicitly configured feature — not the default behavior of the Secret object itself. So a cluster that hasn't turned that on is storing 'secrets' that are one base64-decode away from plaintext for anyone with the right access.

This is why many teams treat the Secret object as a delivery mechanism rather than the actual store: the real secret lives in a dedicated vault with its own access control and audit logging, and Kubernetes either references it (via something like an external-secrets operator syncing the value in) or a sidecar fetches it directly at runtime. That gets you the vault's stronger access control and rotation story while still letting the application consume the value the way it expects.

**Testing:** whether you know the specific mechanical gap (encoding vs. encryption) rather than just repeating 'Secrets aren't fully secure' without being able to say why.

interviewQuestions.question: You're setting security standards for a growing platform team running dozens of services on Kubernetes. How would you make sure hardening practices like non-root containers and network policies actually get applied consistently, rather than depending on every engineer remembering?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I wouldn't rely on documentation and code review catching every case — that scales linearly with review diligence and fails quietly the moment someone's in a hurry. I'd push for **admission control** as the actual enforcement mechanism: policy engines like OPA/Gatekeeper or Kyverno that reject a pod spec at creation time if it violates a rule — running as root, missing resource limits, no NetworkPolicy covering the namespace it's deploying into. That converts the practice from a checklist item into something the cluster mechanically refuses to violate, regardless of who's deploying.

I'd roll this out the same way I'd roll out any enforcement change with teeth: start every new policy in audit/dry-run mode, see what it would have blocked against real traffic and existing deployments, fix the legitimate violations it surfaces, and only then flip it to enforcing — the same staged pattern used for network segmentation or firewall rule changes elsewhere in this area. Flipping straight to blocking on day one against a cluster no one has fully audited is how you cause an unplanned outage instead of a security win.

I'd pair this with image scanning as a CI gate (not just an informational report) and RBAC review as a recurring, not one-time, task — the same 'permission drift' problem from cloud IAM applies just as much to Kubernetes ServiceAccounts. The overall goal is that following the secure path requires no extra discipline from an individual engineer; the insecure path simply isn't available to take.

**Testing:** whether you default to structural, automated enforcement over relying on individual diligence — the pattern that shows up as the mature answer across nearly every topic in this area.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Design

interviewQuestions.question: A pentest finds that a compromised pod in one namespace was able to reach and query a database pod in a completely unrelated namespace. How would you explain how that happened, and how would you fix it?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The most likely explanation is simple and common: Kubernetes networking is flat by default. Unless NetworkPolicy resources explicitly restrict traffic, any pod can reach any other pod on any port regardless of namespace — namespaces are an organizational and RBAC boundary, not a network boundary, on their own. So a compromised pod reaching across namespaces isn't a bug or an exploit of some Kubernetes flaw; it's the default, undisturbed behavior of a cluster that never had default-deny policies written for it.

The fix is writing NetworkPolicies that scope legitimate traffic explicitly and, in the process, make everything else denied by default — once any policy selects a pod, unmatched traffic to it is refused. I'd start with the highest-value targets (databases, anything holding sensitive data) rather than trying to microsegment the whole cluster in one pass, mapping actual observed traffic first so the policy doesn't accidentally break a real dependency nobody documented.

The deeper point I'd bring back to the team: this is the same lateral-movement gap covered for physical networks earlier in this area, just re-appearing inside a cluster instead of across VLANs. A pentest finding this specific gap usually means the org invested in perimeter and image-level controls but hadn't yet applied the microsegmentation mindset to the cluster's own internal network — a common, and very fixable, blind spot.

**Testing:** whether you can connect a Kubernetes-specific finding back to the general segmentation principle, rather than treating it as an isolated Kubernetes quirk.
